newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. massacre probe in Kabila's Congo delayed.
newsitem.headline: U.N. massacre probe in Kabila's Congo delayed.

text.p: A U.N. negotiating team and Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo agreed to differ on Friday on the terms of reference for a major massacre probe, delaying its planned Monday start until further notice.

Members of the U.N. team said progress had been made but that it would be up to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and the members of the Security Council to make the final decision on the best way out of the impasse.

A joint statement, issued simultaneously in Geneva and Kinshasa after two weeks of negotiations, said the two sides disagreed on both the composition of the team and the period the U.N. team will investigate.
"As a consequence, the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo asks the United Nations to redefine the mandate of the inquiry," it added.
"The two parties agreed to bring the results of their discussions to the attention of the U.N. Secretary-General and the U.N. Commission on Human Rights."

The probe follows allegations that Kabila's Tutsi-backed rebels or their Rwandan or Ugandan allies killed Rwandan Hutu refugees as their forces marched across former Zaire before toppling veteran Zairean dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May.
The United Nations is anxious for its forensic experts to excavate mass graves in the east of former Zaire -- before the evidence disappears. Kabila's government denies the allegations.
The breakdown meant that the full investigation is blocked from going ahead on Monday under its existing mandate laid down last April by the 53-member U.N. Commission on Human Rights.
"We cannot do an investigation without the cooperation of the government," John Mills, a member of the team, told Reuters.
"We have not given up. We will continue to push. We have made serious progress," he said. "The next step will be at the level of the secretary-general and the member states."
Kabila's government refuses to accept Chilean lawyer Roberto Garreton, U.N. rapporteur or special investiagtor for the area since 1994, as leader or as a member of the mission.
It wants the team to extend the inquiry beyond October, when its forces took up arms against Mobutu, to March 1993, before the Rwanda genocide of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners.

Most of the Hutu refugees flooded out of Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after armed Tutsis exiles returned and drove out the Hutu hardliners responsible for the genocide. Others fled from the Tutsi-dominated army in neighbouring Burundi.

Annan indicated on Thursday he would be willing to drop Garreton as head of mission if it could clear the way for determining the fate of missing Rwandan Hutu refugees. "The most important thing is for us to get to the facts," he said.
Annan may choose to take the issue before the Security Council, according to U.N. sources in Geneva. "There are other avenues than the Commission," said one.

In April, Garreton accused Kabila's rebels of massacring Hutu refugees in their push across Africa's third largest nation. Garreton's latest report, due out in the next few days, is likely to add fuel to the fire, according to U.N. sources.
The joint statement did not refer to Garreton by name but said: "The government demands that all members of the mission of inquiry have its prior approval".

The two-page statement was signed by Emmanuel Kanbali, head of a government liaison team, and Georg Mautner-Markhof, head of a small U.N. advance team including Argentine forensics which has been seeking agreement on the terms for the full inquiry.
It said "a certain number of principles and practical modalities" on conduct of the probe had been agreed.
Members of the U.N. advance team were to leave by Saturday.
